lessons.title: The Philippine Health Care Delivery System
lessons.subject: NP I – Community Health Nursing
lessons.high_yield_reason: Directly named in the official TOS under NP I; foundational for every other community health topic and frequently tested as structure/who-does-what items.
learning_objectives: Describe the three levels of the Philippine health care delivery system (national, regional, local)
Differentiate the roles of DOH, LGUs, and PhilHealth
Explain how devolution under the Local Government Code shaped current health service delivery
Identify the referral pathway from barangay to tertiary facility
core_concepts: Health care delivery in the Philippines is a devolved, three-tier system: national policy/regulation (DOH), local delivery (LGU-run RHUs, city/municipal health offices), and financing (PhilHealth)
The 1991 Local Government Code devolved basic health service delivery to LGUs; DOH retained stewardship, standard-setting, and specialized/tertiary services

Primary care is delivered through Barangay Health Stations (BHS) and Rural Health Units (RHUs)/City Health Offices; secondary care through district/provincial hospitals; tertiary care through regional/specialty hospitals and medical centers

definitions.definition: Transfer of basic health service responsibility and funding from the national government to LGUs (provinces, cities, municipalities), per the Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160).
The national government agency responsible for health policy, standards, regulation, and stewardship of the health system as a whole.

The Philippine Health Insurance Corporation — the national health insurer, financing coverage under the National Health Insurance Program and, since RA 11223, automatic UHC enrollment for all citizens.

lessons.detailed_explanation: The Philippine health system is organized in tiers that mirror the referral pathway a patient moves through. At the community level, the Barangay Health Station (BHS), typically staffed by a Barangay Health Worker (BHW) and visited periodically by a Rural Health Midwife or Public Health Nurse, is the first point of contact. Above it sits the Rural Health Unit (RHU) in rural areas or the City/Municipal Health Office in urban areas — headed by the Municipal/City Health Officer (a physician) and staffed by public health nurses, midwives, and sanitary inspectors — which delivers primary care and basic preventive/promotive services. Referral from here moves to district or provincial hospitals (secondary care, basic surgical/inpatient capability), then to regional hospitals or medical centers (tertiary care, specialist and subspecialist services). Since devolution under RA 7160 (1991), LGUs (provinces, cities, municipalities) are legally responsible for operating and funding these local facilities, while DOH functions as the national steward — setting policy, standards, technical assistance, and running select national/specialty hospitals directly. PhilHealth sits alongside this structure as the financing arm, reimbursing facilities for covered services.
lessons.clinical_significance: Nurses in both hospital and community settings need to know this pathway to make appropriate referrals, understand why certain services are or aren't available at a given facility level, and to correctly counsel patients/families on where to seek care for their condition and how the referral system is supposed to work.
lessons.medical_management: Not applicable — this is a systems/structure topic, not a clinical condition.

nursing_process.assessment: Community/family assessment of health-seeking behavior, awareness of and access to local facilities, and existing barriers (distance, cost, cultural).
nursing_process.diagnosis: Example: Ineffective health maintenance related to limited access to primary care facilities.
nursing_process.planning: Collaborate with LGU health office and barangay officials to strengthen referral linkages and health education on when/where to seek care.
nursing_process.interventions: Health teaching on the referral system; coordinate with BHWs; strengthen record/referral slip systems.
nursing_process.evaluation: Improved appropriate use of facility levels (e.g., reduced inappropriate ER use for primary-care-level concerns).

patient_education: Where to go first for non-emergency concerns (BHS/RHU, not the hospital)
What documents/referral slips are needed to move up the referral chain
PhilHealth coverage basics relevant to their visit

priority_nursing_actions: Direct patients to the appropriate level of care first (avoid unnecessary tertiary-facility overload)
Ensure proper referral documentation when escalating care

common_exam_angles: Which facility/personnel is responsible for X (e.g., 'Who heads the Rural Health Unit?' → Municipal Health Officer)
What law devolved health services to LGUs → RA 7160, Local Government Code of 1991
Correct referral sequence from barangay to tertiary care
clinical_pearls: DOH = policy/stewardship/national; LGU = actual local service delivery, post-devolution
PhilHealth is financing, not service delivery — don't confuse its role with DOH's
common_mistakes: Confusing DOH's regulatory role with LGUs' operational role
Assuming PhilHealth runs hospitals — it does not; it reimburses/finances care

mnemonics.expansion: Barangay Health Station → Rural Health Unit/City Health Office → District Hospital → Regional Hospital → Tertiary/Medical Center — the referral ladder, smallest to largest.

quick_review: 3 tiers: national (DOH) → local (LGU-run facilities) → financing (PhilHealth)
Devolution = RA 7160, 1991
Referral ladder: BHS → RHU/City Health Office → District/Provincial Hospital → Regional/Tertiary
key_takeaways: DOH sets policy; LGUs deliver care; PhilHealth finances it
Know the referral ladder cold — it's a recurring PNLE structure question
references: RA 7160, Local Government Code of 1991 [VERIFY exact devolved-functions section if quoting statute directly]
Department of Health organizational mandate (doh.gov.ph) [VERIFY current org structure — not fetched this session]

lessons.title: Primary Health Care: Alma-Ata to Universal Health Care (RA 11223)
lessons.subject: NP I – Community Health Nursing
lessons.high_yield_reason: Explicitly named in the official TOS (Primary Health Care/Primary Care under NP I); UHC Act is current, high-priority policy content.
learning_objectives: Explain the philosophy and four A's/elements of Primary Health Care (PHC) from the 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration
Describe the key provisions of RA 11223 (Universal Health Care Act)
Differentiate PHC as a philosophy/strategy versus UHC as a policy/legal framework
Identify the role of nurses in PHC implementation at the community level
core_concepts: PHC, per the 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration, is essential health care made universally accessible through means acceptable to individuals/families, with their full participation, at a cost the community/country can afford

PHC commonly summarized by the '4 A's': Accessibility, Availability, Affordability, Acceptability [🔵 review-center convention framing of the PHC elements, not a verbatim Alma-Ata phrase — useful teaching shorthand]

RA 11223 (Universal Health Care Act, 2019) automatically enrolls every Filipino citizen in the National Health Insurance Program, reorganizes local health systems into 'health care provider networks,' and shifts emphasis toward population-based, primary-care-first delivery

definitions.definition: A philosophy and strategy for organizing health care around accessible, community-participatory, essential services, first formally defined at the 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration (WHO/UNICEF).
A policy goal — and in the Philippines, a specific law (RA 11223) — ensuring all citizens have access to needed quality health services without financial hardship.

lessons.detailed_explanation: PHC and UHC are related but distinct: PHC is the *how* (a care philosophy/strategy centered on accessibility, community participation, and appropriate technology), while UHC is a *policy commitment* (that everyone gets covered, quality care without financial hardship). The Philippines formally embraced PHC starting in the late 1970s/1980s, restructuring rural health delivery around it. RA 11223, signed in 2019, operationalizes UHC domestically: it automatically enrolls all Filipinos in PhilHealth (removing the old distinction between 'members' who paid premiums and the previously uninsured), mandates the creation of integrated 'health care provider networks' organized by province/city to coordinate primary-to-tertiary referral, and pushes a 'primary care first' gatekeeping model where patients are meant to access non-emergency care through a primary care provider before being referred upward.
lessons.clinical_significance: Community health nurses are direct implementers of PHC principles — home visiting, health education, and working through community health workers all operationalize PHC's participatory, accessible-care philosophy. Nurses also need to understand UHC/RA 11223 to correctly advise patients on their now-automatic PhilHealth coverage and the referral-network model.

nursing_process.assessment: Assess community awareness of PhilHealth coverage/UHC entitlements and existing barriers to primary care access.
nursing_process.diagnosis: Example: Deficient knowledge related to unfamiliarity with UHC/PhilHealth entitlements.
nursing_process.planning: Plan community health education sessions on UHC coverage and how to access the local provider network.
nursing_process.interventions: Health teaching, coordination with LGU health office on provider-network navigation, community organizing.
nursing_process.evaluation: Increased appropriate utilization of primary care services; improved understanding of entitlements.

patient_education: All Filipinos are automatically PhilHealth members under RA 11223 — no need to have paid premiums to be covered for certain services
The primary-care-first / gatekeeping model and why going straight to a hospital for non-emergencies may not be the intended pathway

priority_nursing_actions: Correct misinformation about needing to 'enroll' in PhilHealth when coverage is now automatic under UHC

common_exam_angles: Year and origin of PHC → 1978, Alma-Ata Declaration
What law established UHC in the Philippines → RA 11223 (2019)
Distinguishing PHC (philosophy/strategy) from UHC (policy/law) when a question tests conceptual precision
clinical_pearls: If a question asks about the *philosophy*, think PHC/Alma-Ata; if it asks about the *current Philippine law*, think RA 11223/UHC Act.
common_mistakes: Treating PHC and UHC as interchangeable terms on the exam — they test the distinction

mnemonics.expansion: Accessibility, Availability, Affordability, Acceptability [🔵 review-center convention]

quick_review: PHC = philosophy, born 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration
UHC = Philippine policy, RA 11223 (2019)
RA 11223: automatic PhilHealth enrollment + provider networks + primary-care-first model
key_takeaways: Know the Alma-Ata year and RA 11223 cold — both are exact-fact exam bait
PHC = strategy/philosophy; UHC = the legal commitment/policy built on it
references: Republic Act No. 11223, Universal Health Care Act (2019) [VERIFY specific implementing-rules details if quoting directly — not fetched this session]

lessons.title: Epidemiology and Levels of Prevention
lessons.subject: NP I – Community Health Nursing
lessons.high_yield_reason: Explicitly named topic in the official TOS ('Epidemiology, Vital Statistics, Demography'); levels of prevention are a classic, frequently-tested application concept.
learning_objectives: Define epidemiology and its core measures (incidence, prevalence)
Differentiate the three levels of prevention (primary, secondary, tertiary) with concrete community health examples
Explain the epidemiologic triad (agent-host-environment)
Interpret basic vital statistics used in community health (crude birth/death rate, infant mortality rate)
core_concepts: Epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states/events in populations, and the application of this to control health problems

Levels of prevention: Primary (prevent disease before it occurs — e.g., immunization), Secondary (early detection/prompt treatment — e.g., screening), Tertiary (limit disability, rehabilitate after disease has occurred — e.g., stroke rehab)
The epidemiologic triad: Agent (causative factor), Host (the person/population), Environment (external factors influencing exposure) — disease occurs when these three interact

definitions.definition: The number of NEW cases of a disease occurring in a population during a specified time period.
The total number of EXISTING cases (new + old) of a disease in a population at a given point or period in time.
Actions taken to prevent disease/injury before it occurs (e.g., immunization, health education, safe water supply).
Early detection and prompt treatment to halt or slow disease progression (e.g., Pap smear screening, TB sputum screening).
Reducing the impact of established disease/disability through rehabilitation and preventing further complications (e.g., post-stroke physical therapy, diabetic foot care to prevent amputation).

lessons.detailed_explanation: PNLE community health items frequently present a scenario and ask which level of prevention a described nursing action represents. The clearest way to sort them: if the disease/injury hasn't happened yet and the action stops it from starting, it's primary (immunization, handwashing education, prenatal vitamins). If the disease is already present but not yet symptomatic/advanced and the action finds it early, it's secondary (screening — mammogram, sputum exam, newborn screening). If the disease/injury has already caused damage and the action limits further decline or restores function, it's tertiary (diabetic teaching to prevent amputation after diagnosis, stroke rehabilitation, colostomy care teaching). The epidemiologic triad frames outbreak/disease-causation questions: Agent (the pathogen/toxin/factor), Host (susceptibility factors — age, immune status, nutrition), Environment (physical/social/biological surroundings enabling transmission, e.g., contaminated water, crowding).
lessons.clinical_significance: This framework underlies essentially every community health intervention choice tested — knowing which level of prevention a given nursing action falls under is a recurring PNLE question type, and correctly identifying agent-host-environment factors is core to outbreak investigation and control planning.

nursing_process.assessment: Identify at-risk populations and where along the primary-secondary-tertiary continuum they need intervention.
nursing_process.diagnosis: Example: Risk for infection related to lack of immunization access in the community.
nursing_process.planning: Design interventions matched to the correct prevention level for the population's actual risk profile.
nursing_process.interventions: Immunization campaigns (primary), community-wide screening programs (secondary), rehabilitation/support-group linkage (tertiary).
nursing_process.evaluation: Measured via incidence/prevalence trend changes, screening uptake rates, or reduced complication rates.

patient_education: Explain screening purpose/frequency to encourage secondary-prevention uptake (e.g., why routine BP/blood glucose checks matter even when asymptomatic)

priority_nursing_actions: Match the intervention to the correct prevention level — a common source of PNLE distractor traps is offering a correctly-worded action at the wrong level

common_exam_angles: Scenario: 'A nurse teaches a diabetic client foot care to prevent amputation' → tertiary prevention (disease already present, action limits further damage)
Scenario: 'A nurse administers the BCG vaccine to a newborn' → primary prevention
Scenario: 'A nurse conducts a community-wide TB sputum screening' → secondary prevention
clinical_pearls: If the client already HAS the diagnosis and the action is about limiting damage/rehab → automatically tertiary, regardless of how 'preventive' the action sounds.
common_mistakes: Calling any screening-and-treat action 'primary' just because it sounds preventive — screening = secondary by definition

mnemonics.mnemonic: Primary = Prevent, Secondary = Screen/Spot early, Tertiary = Treat the damage/Rehab

quick_review: Primary = before disease exists (immunization, education)
Secondary = early detection (screening)
Tertiary = limiting damage/rehab after disease is established
Triad = Agent + Host + Environment
key_takeaways: Prevention-level scenario questions are one of the most recurring NP I item types — practice sorting scenarios fast
Incidence = new cases; Prevalence = all existing cases
references: Standard community health nursing curriculum framework (Leavell & Clark levels of prevention model) [🔵 widely used teaching model, standard across PH nursing schools, not a PRC-issued document]

lessons.title: Community Organizing Participatory Action Research (COPAR)
lessons.subject: NP I – Community Health Nursing
lessons.high_yield_reason: Explicitly named as its own topic in the official TOS; was completely missing from the original v1 outline draft, confirmed gap.
learning_objectives: Define COPAR and its underlying philosophy
Sequence the phases of COPAR correctly
Identify the nurse's role at each COPAR phase
Differentiate COPAR from a routine community health assessment
core_concepts: COPAR is a social development approach used in Philippine community health practice that empowers communities to identify their own problems and mobilize their own resources to address them, rather than having solutions imposed externally

🟢 CORRECTED (was previously listed as 3 phases — verified via web search against multiple Philippine nursing-school course materials, consistently confirmed): COPAR has FOUR official phases — (1) Pre-Entry, (2) Entry/Social Preparation, (3) Organization-Building, and (4) Sustenance and Strengthening. The 'Organization-Building' phase (where trained leaders/core groups are formally structured into a functioning community organization) is distinct from Entry and was missing in the original draft.

The nurse's/organizer's role shifts across phases from external facilitator/catalyst (Pre-Entry/Entry) to trainer/capacity-builder (Organization-Building) to advisory/eventual withdrawal as the community sustains its own leadership structures (Sustenance and Strengthening)

definitions.definition: Community Organizing Participatory Action Research — a continuous, participatory process of educating and mobilizing communities to identify and act on their own health and development needs.

A small group of community leaders/volunteers identified and trained early in COPAR (Entry phase) to help lead the organizing process from within the community; formally structured into an organization during the Organization-Building phase.

lessons.detailed_explanation: COPAR distinguishes itself from a standard community health assessment by its emphasis on community self-determination — the nurse or health worker acts as a facilitator/catalyst, not the decision-maker. (1) Pre-Entry: the organizer/institution selects a project site, conducts preliminary social investigation, and prepares staff/host arrangements before any community contact. (2) Entry/Social Preparation: the organizer integrates with the community (living among and absorbing their lifestyle), runs an information campaign, deepens the social investigation, provides basic health services as an entry point, and identifies potential leaders — this phase is sometimes described as 'conscientization,' helping people realize they have the capacity to understand and change their own situation. (3) Organization-Building: identified leaders and core groups are formally trained (formal, informal, and on-the-job training) and structured into a functioning, community-wide organization capable of managing its own concerns and programs. (4) Sustenance and Strengthening: the established community organization independently plans, implements, and evaluates its own programs — training members to monitor/implement health programs, identifying new leaders, building partnerships, and initiating livelihood projects — with the original organizer's role reduced to overall guidance rather than direct leadership.
lessons.clinical_significance: COPAR is directly examined as a community health methodology distinct from clinical nursing process; PNLE items testing this usually give a scenario describing a specific organizing activity and ask which COPAR phase it represents, or ask about the nurse's appropriate role at that phase.

nursing_process.assessment: Community integration and secondary-data review before formal entry.
nursing_process.diagnosis: Not a clinical nursing diagnosis context — COPAR uses community-identified problems/priorities instead.
nursing_process.planning: Co-planned with the community core group, not unilaterally by the health worker.
nursing_process.interventions: Core group formation and training, participatory community diagnosis, mobilization for community-identified priority actions.
nursing_process.evaluation: Sustainability of community-led structures after the organizer withdraws.

patient_education: Not applicable in the traditional 1:1 sense — COPAR education is community/group-level capacity building

priority_nursing_actions: Avoid imposing the nurse's own priorities over community-identified priorities — this violates COPAR's core philosophy and is a common wrong-answer trap on exam items

common_exam_angles: Scenario ordering: which COPAR activity comes first (pre-entry secondary data review vs. core group formation)
Distinguishing the nurse's facilitator role from a directive 'expert' role
clinical_pearls: If an exam option has the nurse deciding/imposing a solution rather than facilitating the community's own decision, it's very likely the wrong answer in a COPAR context.
common_mistakes: Treating COPAR as identical to a routine windshield survey/community assessment — COPAR is specifically about organizing for community self-mobilization, not just data collection

mnemonics.expansion: Pre-entry → Entry/social preparation → Organization-building → Sustenance & strengthening (4 phases, confirmed)

quick_review: COPAR = community self-mobilization, not externally imposed solutions
4 phases: Pre-Entry → Entry (Social Preparation) → Organization-Building → Sustenance and Strengthening
Nurse role: facilitator/catalyst → integrator → trainer/capacity-builder → advisory/withdrawal
Core group = locally trained leaders who are formally organized in the Organization-Building phase
key_takeaways: COPAR is philosophy-driven — 'who decides' matters as much as 'what is decided' on exam items
COPAR has 4 phases, not 3 — Organization-Building is a distinct, commonly-tested phase between Entry and Sustenance
references: Nurseslabs, 'Community Organizing Participatory Action Research (COPAR)' — https://nurseslabs.com/copar-community-organizing-participatory-action-research/ (verified via web search; consistent with multiple Philippine nursing-school course materials, e.g. Bukidnon State University, Central Mindanao University, Cavite State University community health nursing course documents)

🟡 Original source of the COPAR methodology is Philippine community organizing/social work literature (associated with institutions such as UP College of Social Work and Community Development); the specific originating academic citation was not directly retrieved this session — the phase structure above is corroborated across multiple independent PH nursing-school sources, but the primary originating document is not yet directly cited

lessons.title: The Family as Client: Normal Family vs. Family at Risk
lessons.subject: NP I – Community Health Nursing
lessons.high_yield_reason: Explicitly split in the official TOS into 'Care of Normal Families' vs. 'Families at Risk' — a confirmed structural distinction that was collapsed/generic in the original v1 outline.
learning_objectives: Apply the nursing process to the family as the unit of care
Differentiate a 'normal'/well family from a 'family at risk'
Identify common family health risk indicators used in community health nursing
Prioritize family nursing problems using a structured approach
core_concepts: In community health nursing, the family — not just the individual — is frequently the primary unit of care, since family dynamics, resources, and behavior directly shape individual health outcomes

A 'family at risk' is one with identifiable factors that increase vulnerability to illness, injury, or crisis (e.g., presence of a communicable disease case, a pregnant teen, a family member with a chronic untreated illness, overcrowding, poor sanitation access, family violence)
Family nursing care plans use the same nursing process (Assessment–Diagnosis–Planning–Intervention–Evaluation) applied at the family-unit level rather than only the individual level

definitions.definition: A family unit with one or more identifiable health/social factors that increase its vulnerability to illness, disability, or crisis, requiring closer nursing follow-up and intervention.
Systematic assessment of a family's structure, function, resources, and specific risk indicators used to prioritize which families need closer community health nursing follow-up.

lessons.detailed_explanation: Community health nurses typically triage caseloads by identifying which families are 'at risk' and require closer, more frequent follow-up versus 'normal'/well families who need routine health promotion contact only. Common at-risk indicators taught in PH community health nursing include: presence of a communicable disease case in the household (e.g., active TB), a family member who is pregnant (especially teen pregnancy or high-risk pregnancy), infants/young children (higher vulnerability), a family member with an unmanaged chronic illness, overcrowded or unsanitary housing, lack of access to safe water, family violence/abuse, and significant economic deprivation. Prioritization within a caseload commonly follows criteria such as: problems that are actual (not just potential) come before potential problems; problems affecting more family members are prioritized over those affecting one member; and problems the family itself recognizes as urgent are typically prioritized to preserve their participation and buy-in.
lessons.clinical_significance: This underlies how community health nurses allocate limited home-visiting time/resources across a barangay caseload, and is directly tested as prioritization-style PNLE items (given several families, which does the nurse visit first?).

assessment.diagnostics: Family health risk appraisal / family assessment tools covering structure, function, resources, and specific risk indicators.

nursing_process.assessment: Family structure (genogram), function, resources, environment, and specific risk indicators (communicable disease, pregnancy, chronic illness, safety).
nursing_process.diagnosis: Example: Risk for infection transmission related to an active TB case within the household.
nursing_process.planning: Prioritize families/problems using actual-before-potential and number-of-members-affected criteria.
nursing_process.interventions: Home visits, health teaching tailored to the specific risk, referral to appropriate services.
nursing_process.evaluation: Reduction in identified risk indicators over successive visits; resolution or stabilization of the at-risk status.

patient_education: Tailored to the specific risk identified (e.g., TB DOTS adherence teaching for a household with an active case, prenatal care importance for a family with a pregnant member)

priority_nursing_actions: When given multiple families in a scenario, visit the one with an ACTUAL, more urgent, and more widely-affecting problem first — this is the classic PNLE prioritization pattern for this topic

common_exam_angles: 'Which family should the community health nurse visit first?' prioritization scenarios comparing several households
Identifying which listed factor makes a family 'at risk' vs. a distractor that sounds concerning but isn't a recognized risk indicator
clinical_pearls: Actual problem > potential problem; problem affecting many members > problem affecting one; communicable/infectious risk to others often outranks a risk contained to one individual
common_mistakes: Prioritizing by severity of diagnosis alone without considering whether the problem is actual vs. potential, or how many family members are affected

quick_review: Family = unit of care in community health nursing, not just the individual
At-risk indicators: communicable disease, pregnancy (esp. teen/high-risk), chronic illness, unsafe housing/water, violence, poverty
Prioritize: actual > potential; multiple members affected > single member; family-recognized urgency matters
key_takeaways: Family nursing prioritization scenarios are a recurring, high-yield NP I item type — practice ranking multiple-family scenarios
The TOS explicitly separates 'normal family' content from 'family at risk' content — expect both framings on the exam
references: Standard Philippine community/family health nursing curriculum content [🔵 broadly consistent across PH nursing textbooks; exact prioritization-criteria wording can vary by source — treat the general logic as reliable, exact phrasing as approximate]

lessons.title: Disaster Nursing: Community Preparedness and Response
lessons.subject: NP I – Community Health Nursing
lessons.high_yield_reason: Explicitly named in the official TOS ('Care of the Community During Disaster'); the Philippines' high disaster exposure makes this consistently relevant/tested content.
learning_objectives: Sequence the phases of the disaster management cycle
Identify the nurse's role at each disaster phase
Apply triage principles in a mass-casualty/disaster context
Describe community-level disaster preparedness planning
core_concepts: 🟢 CORRECTED (verified via web search against RA 10121 text, its NDRRMP 2011–2028, and NDRRMC official documents): the Philippines' legal disaster framework does NOT use the generic single-word 'Mitigation/Preparedness/Response/Recovery' model. RA 10121 (Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010) officially defines FOUR PAIRED thematic areas: (1) Disaster Prevention and Mitigation, (2) Disaster Preparedness, (3) Disaster Response, and (4) Disaster Rehabilitation and Recovery — each led by a designated NDRRMC member-agency and corresponding NDRRMC committee.

The generic international 4-phase disaster-cycle model (Mitigation/Preparedness/Response/Recovery) is still useful as a conceptual scaffold and is what most general/international nursing textbooks teach, but on a PNLE item testing Philippine-specific law, the officially correct terminology is the RA 10121 paired-thematic-area wording above

Community health nurses have distinct roles at each RA 10121 thematic area — from hazard mapping and public education (prevention and mitigation/preparedness) to triage and emergency care coordination (response) to psychosocial support and rebuilding health services (rehabilitation and recovery)

START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) is a commonly taught mass-casualty triage method sorting victims into categories (commonly color-coded: immediate/red, delayed/yellow, minor/green, expectant or deceased/black) [🔵 START is a widely-used, standard emergency/disaster triage teaching framework; this session's research did not confirm it as an explicit DOH/PH-mandated protocol name, so treat it as generally-taught convention rather than confirmed PH statute]

definitions.definition: RA 10121's official first thematic area — actions taken to avoid or reduce the long-term risk of a disaster's impact before it occurs (e.g., building codes, hazard mapping, land-use planning restricting development in high-hazard zones).

RA 10121's official second thematic area — planning and readiness activities conducted in advance of a disaster to ensure effective response (e.g., evacuation drills, stockpiling supplies, training, early warning systems).

RA 10121's official fourth thematic area — the long-term process of rebuilding communities after a disaster: restoring infrastructure and health services, and implementing measures to prevent/reduce future disaster impact.
The process of sorting casualties by urgency/survivability to allocate limited resources to those who will benefit most, especially in mass-casualty situations.

lessons.detailed_explanation: RA 10121 restructured the former National Disaster Coordinating Council into the NDRRMC and organizes all national disaster policy around four official thematic areas, each with its own lead agency and NDRRMC committee: (1) Disaster Prevention and Mitigation — hazard/vulnerability mapping, risk assessments, land-use and infrastructure standards; community health nurses may contribute to hazard mapping and health-risk advocacy here. (2) Disaster Preparedness — developing and rehearsing community disaster/evacuation plans, stockpiling supplies, training, and early warning systems; nurses conduct public education (e.g., 'go-bag' contents, evacuation routes) and help build local DRRM capacity. (3) Disaster Response — the phase most textbooks focus on for direct clinical action: search and rescue support, emergency medical services, field triage, first aid, coordinating evacuation-center health services, and communicable-disease surveillance in crowded shelters (a major post-disaster risk in the Philippines given frequent typhoon-driven evacuations). (4) Disaster Rehabilitation and Recovery — restoring routine health services, psychosocial support for trauma, and rebuilding damaged health infrastructure, alongside longer-term risk-reduction measures to prevent recurrence. Under mass-casualty triage systems like START, the sickest-but-savable victims (immediate/red) are treated first; those with injuries that can wait (delayed/yellow) next; walking wounded (minor/green) last among survivors; and victims not expected to survive given available resources are categorized separately (expectant/black) — a deliberately different logic from normal individual patient prioritization, since disaster triage optimizes survival across the whole casualty group rather than any one patient.
lessons.clinical_significance: The Philippines' high exposure to typhoons, earthquakes, and floods makes disaster nursing directly practice-relevant, not just exam content — and PNLE tests both the phase-sequencing knowledge and the ethically distinct logic of mass-casualty triage versus routine individual-patient prioritization.

nursing_process.assessment: Community hazard/vulnerability assessment; post-disaster rapid needs assessment of the affected population.
nursing_process.diagnosis: Example: Risk for infection related to overcrowded evacuation center conditions.
nursing_process.planning: Develop/rehearse community disaster plans; plan surge capacity and shelter health services.
nursing_process.interventions: Triage, first aid, disease surveillance in shelters, psychosocial first aid, health education.
nursing_process.evaluation: Reduced morbidity/mortality; effective resource allocation; community resilience post-recovery.

patient_education: Family/community disaster preparedness planning: go-bags, evacuation routes, family reunification plans

complications: Communicable disease outbreaks in crowded evacuation centers
Mental health impact/trauma in affected populations
Disruption of routine health services (immunization, prenatal care, chronic disease management) post-disaster
